To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the macrophages of mice hyperimmunised against a syngeneic lymphoma are larger and more active than normal macrophages and 2) when mixed in vitro with lymphoma cells they exhibit a greater increase in acid phosphatase and lysosomal fusion.

(1) macrophages from immunized mice have more small lysosomes than macrophages from non-immunized mice; (2) macrophages and lymphoma cells interact in vitro; (3) macrophages have an effect on lymphoma cell growth; and (4) the interaction of macrophages and tumor cells results in the appearance of small lysosomes and their fusion.

the interaction of immune and non-immune macrophages with syngeneic lymphoma cells results in the appearance of small lysosomes in IPM and in the formation of large lysosomes by fusion of small lysosomes.

the interaction between syngeneic immune peritoneal macro-phages and L 5178Y cells.
the study of the interaction between syngeneic immune peritoneal macro phages (IPM), obtained by hyperimmunization against syngenei c L 5178Y lymphoma cells, and normal peritoneal macro-phages (NPM).
the mechanisms of macrophage-mediated cytotoxicity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IPM and N 17 8 Y cells interact to form a complex, which is followed by a series of events that are characteristic of the macrophage.
there are no specific ultrastructural or biochemical changes in IPM which could account for their ability to specifically recognize and destroy L 5178Y tumour cells.
there is a specific recognition between IPM and L5178Y cells which leads to the activation of IPM, the production of acid hydrolases and subsequent lysosomal fusion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

IPM and NIM have similar ultrastructural characteristics but that IPM have more acid phosphatase and that the IPM have an enhanced ability to fuse their lysosomes in response to the tumour target cells.

the interaction between the macrophages and the lymphoma cells in vitro is not an all or none phenomenon, that the macrophages can be activated by tumour antigens, and that there are differences in the activation process between syngeneic and allogeneic tumour cells.

IPM have an inherent capacity for lysosomal fusion and that they are capable of lysosomal acid hydrolase production in the absence of tumour cell stimulation, but that the rate and degree of this production is dependent on tumour stimulation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
macrophages are a heterogeneous population of cells and the activation of the macrophages is not an all or none event.

the IPM were able to inhibit the proliferation of L 517Y cells in vitro by a process which involved the formation of a strong adhesion between the two cell types and the release of lysosomal enzymes into the tumour cells.
IPM are more efficient in lysosomal fusion than NPM and that the increase in acid phosphatase is probably not a direct consequence of fusion.
